card.keepWhy: The real you isn’t worn out. Only the clothes are.
sources: Bhagavad Gita 2.22 (as a person casts off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, so the embodied self casts off worn-out bodies and enters new ones)
Bhagavad Gita 2.23-24 (weapons do not cut the self, fire does not burn it, water does not wet it, wind does not dry it)
Bhagavad Gita, chapter 2 setting: Arjuna’s grief at the thought of losing people he loves in battle
check: The verse is about death and rebirth; the lesson and film also apply it to habits and labels (“old outfits”). Confirm this gentle application is acceptable.

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? do you ever feel worn out, like an old version of yourself? tired, stuck, same old you.
options: then this picture is for you. listen.
then keep this one for those days. listen.
good. listen anyway, it’s a lovely one.

steps.line: In the Gita, Krishna gives Arjuna a simple picture.

steps.q: Krishna’s picture is changing clothes. What do you guess he says about the old ones?
o: They’re set aside once they’re worn out
They’re passed on to someone younger
They’re burned, so nothing is left
steps.why: Gita 2.22. Krishna’s word is jirnani: worn out, old with use. You don’t mourn a shirt that has done its work; you change it.

steps.line: Just as a person sets aside worn-out clothes, and puts on new ones,

steps.q: Who is Krishna to Arjuna at this moment?
steps.why: Krishna is driving Arjuna’s chariot, and is also his cousin. The whole Gita is a talk between two armies: the friend at the reins and the warrior who can’t go on.

steps.line: so the soul leaves a worn-out body behind, and takes on a new one.

steps.q: Krishna says this to Arjuna, who is grieving the people he might lose. Why would this picture comfort him?
o: It says death doesn’t really happen
It says the true self outlasts the body
It says grief is a weakness to hide
steps.why: Krishna doesn’t say bodies won’t die. He says the one wearing them isn’t destroyed (2.20). Many Hindus hear this verse read at funerals.

steps.line: In Hindu thought, the real you, the atman, is never worn out, never damaged, never old.
steps.label: atman

steps.q: Atman is often translated “soul.” Many scholars link the word to something older. What?
steps.why: Many link atman to an old word for breath, like German atmen. In use it simply means self: the real you.

steps.line: The real you isn’t worn out. Only the clothes are.
steps.label: today

say: here’s what i love. in krishna’s picture, nothing about the real you gets old. only the clothes do.
in hindu thought the atman, the true self, can’t be cut, burned or worn out. bodies, moods and labels change. the one wearing them stays whole.

steps.q: Krishna also says no weapon can cut the atman, and no fire can burn it. So what can a hard year, or an old label, really touch?
o: Only the clothes, never the one wearing them
The atman, a little at a time
Nothing at all, so nothing ever changes
steps.why: Hard years wear out clothes. They can’t wear out you. That’s why a fresh start is always possible.

today.say: name one “old outfit” you’re ready to take off: a habit, a label, a story about yourself. write it down, then set it aside, like a worn-out shirt.
options: then set it aside today. the real you is fine.
It feels like who I am
worn long enough, clothes feel like skin. they still aren’t you.
